Mr. OLIVER moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 186) to amend the Irrigation Act. He said: There are two distinct provisions in this Act. One is an amendment to the amendments that were made the session before last. Drainage is deemed to foe a function of the provincial government, and while the Irrigation Act places the control in the three provinces in the hands of the Dominion, the amendments of the session of 1908 permit drainage works to be carried on under provincial jurisdiction, subject to certain requirements.
Does the Act apply to British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, only to the three prairie provinces. The governments of the two western provinces find that, in dealing with drainage, there are two classes-the least important and the most important; and the amendment is simply to enable us to dispense wdth the filing of elaborate plans in the case of minor drainage schemes authorized by the provincial government. The other provision is to authorize expro-piration where necessary for Teservoir sites for the purpose of conserving water for irrigation. There is a provision already for preservation of such sites where the land is the property of the Crown, but- in some cases some part of it may have passed into private hands, and that small part might render useless the reservation of the rest.

The nice question arises here as to the jurisdiction of this parliament to legislate at all with reference to irrigation. When the Bill comes up for its second reading, we ought to have the opinion of the Minister of Justice.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: WATER-POWER IN THE BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY BELT.

speechtext: Mr. OLIVER moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 187) to confirm and declare the rights of the Crown with respect to water and water-power and relating to the diversion, acquisition ana use of water in the railway belt in British Columbia. He said: As the House is aware, the proprietary rights in a belt 20 miles in width on each side of the main line on the Canadian Pacific railway, where it passes through the province of British Columbia, has, under an arrangement between the Dominion and the province, become the - property of the Crown in the right of the Dominion. Up to a time, it was assumed that the province administered all water rights within that area as well as throughout the rest of the province. However, a couple of years ago, a case was entered in the Exchequer Court for the purpose of deciding definitely whether the jurisdiction in regard to water within the railway belt resided in the Crown in the right of the province or in the Crown in the right of the Dominion. The Exchequer Court gave a decision that the right rested with the Dominion. Since then, I am given to understand, the Supreme Court, on appeal, has confirmed the decision of the Exchequer Court. Of course, in order to reach a final conclusion tne matter will have to be carried to the Privy Council, and that decision will be the one that will rule. In the meantime, the rights to water which have been granted by the provincial government are in a state of uncertainty. The provincial government having been declared to have no right in this matter, grants issued by that government have not-to put it mildly-a satisfactory legal status. The purpose of this Bill, then, is, first to declare, in accordance with the decision of the court, that the right to the water rests in the Dominion, and, second, to make provision for carrying forward the rights which have been granted by the provincial government until they can be readjusted or until a final decision is reached. It is for the purpose of preventing or avoiding a practically chaotic condition in regard to water rights in the railway belt so as to put them on a definite basis during the interval which necessarily occurs between the first decision of the Exchequer Court and the final decision of the Privy Council. At the same time, there is a demand for development in the railway belt, and it is proposed in the same Act to make provision for authorizing development as the circumstances may require, so, that in the first place, the rights granted shall not be in a state of chaos, and, in the next place, development need not be tied up awaiting the decision of the Privy Council.

speechtext: It is an interesting question that the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) has raised. On the second reading of the Bill, of course, we can discuss it fully. He states that by a decision of the Exchequer Court, confirmed by the Supreme Court, the right to legislate in reference to lands which have been conveyed to the Dominion is given to the Dominion parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WATER-POWER IN THE BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY BELT.
speechtext: In water rights.

maintopic: WATER-POWER IN THE BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY BELT.
speechtext: In reference to water rights, or any other. That is a power vested in the provincial authority, and I doubt very much if any court in the land has decided that, by the conveying of the land to the Dominion government, the right to legislate for that area is thereby conveyed to the Dominion. The Dominion can, either by regulation or by Act of parliament, decide on what terms the right conveyed to it-which is no greater right than that which is conveyed to an individual-shall be exercised. But the right of regulation, the right of legislation in reference to these lands, is in the provincial government, and by no conveyance of land can that right be transferred to the Dominion.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 188) to amend the Act respecting the National Battlefields at Quebec. He said:	The purpose of this Bill is to
remove some of the practical difificulties which the commission having charge of the National Battlefields at Quebec have experienced under the statute, by which they were created two years ago. Provision is made in that statute that, in case it is desired to acquire property which has to be expropriated, the provisions of the Railway Act are to be followed. But a literal compliance with the provisions of the Railway Act, with regard to the expropriation of property, would necessitate the filing of plans and the taking of other formal steps which are scarcely applicable to the circumstances of the acquisition of property for the purposes of the National Battlefields Commission. To get rid of that difficulty, and to provide a more ready, and as we think, a more efficient means for carrying out the purposes for which the commission was constituted, this Bill proposes to repeal that section of the original statute and to substitute for it the section contained in the Bill, under which the provisions of the Expropriation Act will be followed. The original statute con-

stituting the commission requires that all propositions for the acquisition of real estate, before being acted upon by the commission, shall be sanctioned by parliament. The effect of the change in procedure which this Bill, if adopted, will in troduce, will merely be that, after parliament has given its approval to the proposition to acquire any particular piece of property for the purposes of the commission, the proceedings, in case expropriation is necessary, shall be in accordance with the general provisions of the expropriation Act, and the price of the property to be paid by the commission shall be settled by proceedings taken in the Exchequer Court.

Before the orders of the day are called, I wish to ask a question of the government. In doing so, I wish to say that while I do not represent the opposition, which is now being led by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. J. Haggart), and the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule"), and while it is distinctly understood that I represent only myself, still I believe that every hon. gentleman around me will back me up. I desire to ask the government whether they are in a position to give the House and the country some definite statement before we adjourn for Easter in regard to tariff negotiations with the United States. This House is about to separate for a week, and will not re-assem-ble until the day before the time fixed for the application of the maximum clauses of the United States tariff to Canada, if they are to be applied. Does not the government consider that it is due to the business community of this country to give some indication as to whether we are to expect a tariff war or not? I wish to assure the government that the members of this House on both sides of it, I believe, are behind the government, provided they stand_ to their guns and do not give away one iota of our rights. I understand that the whole matter is dependent upon the importation of pulp-wood free into the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid that, with every desire on my part to inform my hon. friend and the House generally of what they naturally desire to know in this matter, I am not in a position to give any statement to my hon. friend. He will no doubt understand that in negotiations of the character which it is known are now in progress, it would be impolitic in the highest degree to make any statement until a conclusion has been reached. At the conclusion of the conference which I had the honour to hold with the president of the United States in Albany, a brief statement was given out in these words: ' The president and Mr. Fielding have been in conference, and while no conclusion has been reached, the matter remains as one of friendly negotiation.' That was the condition at that moment, and that is the condition to-day. I am very hopeful that an early arrangement will be reached. But I can assure my hon. friend that I do not think any good purpose would be served by our making any further Mr. WALLACE.
statement on that subject to-day. I am satisfied that the desire he has and that we have is the same, and he will agree with me, on reflection, that it would only be embarrassing the situation for the government to make any statement at this stage.

If the House will allow me to make one remark, I wish to assure the hon. the Minister of Finance that we are behind him in standing by the guns of Canada in this matter. While I realize that perhaps he would not feel at liberty to give any information on certain points, still he must remember, and the Prime Minister may be assured, that in so far as they stand by Canada in this matter we are behind them irrespective of party. 1 wish to say this also
The hon. gentleman cannot enter into a discussion after he has put the question.
I merely wish to state to the minister my intention of giving him

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I accept my hon. friend's statement.
I want to say to the minister that I am with him.

Before my hon. friend (Mr. Lewis) had propounded his question, I had taken the liberty of sending a memorandum to the Minister of Finance on a question I proposed to ask him, and which I do not think will involve the disclosure of any state secrets. I wish to ask the Finance Minister this question: Having regard to the fact that parliament is now in session, will the Finance Minister assure the House that he will not agree to admit the United States to participation in the intermediate tariff, or otherwise substantially to alter the tariff conditions between Canada and the United States, without first submitting the proposals to parliament? I do not think an answer to that question would involve the disclosure of any secret, but it will enable us to understand that we shall be consulted before anything is done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am obliged to my hon. friend for his courtesy in sending me in advance a notice of his question. I agree that an answer to it would not involve the disclosure of any secret, but it *would involve a declaration of policy, which I think would rather embarrass the freedom of negotiations which we desire that the government should have. I must ask my hon. friends on both sides of the House rather to assume that the government are thoroughly seized of the importance of the whole question, and are dealing with it in the manner which they conceive to be consistent with the best interests of Canada. I do not think my hon. friend, on reflection,

will feel that he ought to press this question. In respect to what has been said by the hon. member for Huron (Mr. Lewis), I may say that if there are to be any guns in the matter, we will be exceedingly glad to have the hon. gentleman along with us behind the guns. But if we can avoid the use of guns at all, that will be much better.

Before we separate for the holidays, I want to ask the government a question about the probable length of the session. When we go home, no doubt many questions will be put to us as to the prob-r able duration of the session, and consequently I would, like to ask the First Minister if he is in a position to give us any information with regard to what measures the government propose to put through, and what others they propose to bring down, any information which will enable us to estimate more closely how long the balance of the session is likely to last.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am glad to say to my hon. friend that any additional programme of business we shall lay before the House will be of a very light character. We shall have some supplementary estimates for the coming year; we shall have resolutions about dry-docks, and we may have some other matters which at the present time I am not at liberty to disclose. But on the whole, I think there is nothing to prevent us from having a very early prorogation.
Is it the intention to go on with the Insurance Act and the Banking Bill? These are two important measures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Although the Insurance Bill is a lengthy Bill, it is one which the House considered last year with great care, and this year the Senate has also given it a great deal of attention, and I think it is in such good shape that we can deal with it without its delaying us much. I am beginning to despair of getting the Bank Act through, and if there is no reasonable chance of getting it through this session, it will stand over until the beginning of next session.

I wish to ask the Prime Minister as to the progress that is being made by the committee appointed by himself for the revision of the rules of this House for the purpose of shortening the sessions. There is a strong feeling in reference to the matter through the country, and I would impress upon the Prime Minister the necessity of something being done this session in regard to revising the rules, which are now a hundred years behind the times.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am able to say to my hon. friend (Mr. Lewis) that we had a meeting of that committee this morning. We shall have another meeting almost immediately after the recess, and in the meantime I will be very glad to receive all communications that come to me from my hon. friend suggesting amendments to the rules.
But does the Prime Minister promise anything?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will be very glad to promise every possible consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) to an article in reference to a complaint from the publisher of 'Cotton's Weekly.' He claims that his paper is being unjustly discriminated against. I put certain questions of the order paper on the 2nd of March to which the Postmaster General replied, but his reply does not seem to

be satisfactory to the publishers of this paper. I would draw his attention to one part of an editorial written in reply to the Postmaster General which is as follows:
Do you not know that the Montreal ' Star ' and 'Witness' and the Toronto 'World,' ' Globe ' and ' Telegram ' are sending bundles of their papers through the mails to parties who order an occasional bundle at a rate sixteen times lower than what you are compelling me to pay? Are you not aware that every little local paper is doing the same thing whenever occasion arises?
I have no interest- in these matters beyond a desire to see fair play, justice and equity meted out to all publishers alike. I suppose there is a provision in the Post Office Act which allows the thing to be done under certain conditions. What I would like to know is how the Postmaster General learns what papers, when sending bundles, keep within the letter of the law and what papers do not? How does he know that a 'Globe' bundle, or a 'World' bundle, is all right and the bundle of the poor man's paper all wrong? Can 'sample' bundles be sent by the rich man's paper, while the poor man's paper for doing the same thing is an outlaw? Is one supposed to be respectable and the other assumed to be disreputable?

I need not say that I bear no ill will to the publisher of ' Cotton's Weekly '. That gentleman seems to be under the impression that the department is discriminating against his paper. Such is not the case. I have fully explained to Mr. Cotton, and to his many friends in the country that there is no discrimination, but that we are simply putting his paper under the ordinary regulations of the department. But Mr. Cotton has started a campaign against the department, and against the minister. I have nothing to say about that except what I have already stated in the House. Since I made that statement to the House the other day, which I need not repeat, because my hon. friend will find it in ' Hansard ', Mr. Cotton in his paper has made a statement in regard to the accusation of discrimination against his paper. I find there is an affidavit from his business manager, in which it is stated that:
I, tbe undersigned, H. A. Webb, business manager of ' Cotton's Weekly,' being duly sworn, do depose and say: Not being a subscriber to tbe undermentioned newspapers, and not being engaged in tbe business of a news agency, I did send for a special bundle of the following five papers, namely, the Montreal 'Daily Star,' the Montreal 'Daily AVitness,' the Toronto ' Daily Globe,' the Toronto ' Daily World,' and the Toronto ' Daily Telegram,' for each of their issue of March 1, 1910.
And he adds further that these papers came in bundles to him without hearing the Mr. HERRON.
address of any one inside. Well, I do not dispute this statement. It may be quite true that a gentleman might have asked these various offices to send a dozen of each of these papers. The House will notice that these are all well known papers having, in every part of Canada, a very large number of subscribers. I might explain to the House that papers, such as the Toronto ' Mail ', Toronto ' Globe ', Montreal ' Star '. or the Montreal ' Witness ', are first sent to the post offices as they have a very large circulation, the post offices have excess to their lists of subscribers, and the papers settle their accounts with the post office. But we do not affix the stamps on each parcel because we would have to use . too large a quantity of stamps for that; so that it may happen that in.a case like this a bundle is sent without bearing the individual addresses of the subscribers, because there is such a large quantity of these papers in the post office in such cities as Toronto, Montreal, Quebec, Halifax, or Winnipeg.
Is it not a fact that all these papers are sent in bundles to news agents all over the country?

Yes, and there is a proviso in the law by which the news agent benefits by the special rate. But the case of Mr. Cotton is radically different. In the first place he has comparatively few subscribers, but he sends his paper to friends who distribute it. The rule of the department is that a paper must have bona fide subscribers, and where the paper is sent them in bundles the rate is one quarter of a cent per pound. As reards this narti-cular case I am not satisfied; probably there may be a mistake. I want to know the circumstances of each case, and I have written to the postmistress at Cowansville where the bundles were received. The fol-following letter was sent out to-day to the postmistress:
The postmistress will find herewith a clipping taken from ' Cotton's Weekly ' of 17th March, and her attention is particularly called to the following paragraphs:-
That I particularly called the attention of the postmaster of Cowansville to the fact that no postage stamps are affixed, and that he held up said bundles until he could communicate with his superior postal authorities.
That the said bundles were later delivered to me without postage stamps affixed, evidently upon the direct instructions of the superior postal authorities.	.
There is no record in the department of any communication from the postmistress upon the subject referred to, nor any instructions having been given. The department desires to be informed whether the statements referred to in this clipping are correct; if so, to whom the postmistress wrote for instructions; and to furnish the department with copies of any instructions she may have received from any officer connected with the postal service.

As the postmistress is aware, the duty of seeing that proper postage is paid upon newspapers and periodicals rests with the postmaster at the office where they are posted, and not with the office of delivery, unless any packages have specially been marked as short paid, when, of course, it is the duty of the delivering office to see that the deficient postage noted on the parcel is properly collected before delivery is made. If, however, the postmaster at any post office of delivery has reasonable grounds for believing that copies of newspapers and periodicals recognized as entitled to statutory postal privileges are being received at his office for delivery at a cheaper rate of postage than should properly be paid, it is the duty of the postmaster at once to notify the department of each instance, if possible procuring the wrappers upon which the address appears, so that steps may be taken by the department to properly investigate each case.
If a newspaper, for instance, the ' Globe,' sends a bundle of newspapers by post to a news agent in Lindsay, is that prepaid?
Yes, it is prepaid.
I understood the Postmaster General to say that when a bundle is sent in cases like that, a list of subscribers to whom the papers are delivered is furnished.
Yes.

But most of these news agents receive a large number of papers in addition to those for subscribers, which are sold over the counter. The list cannot be reliable, because the number will change perhaps twice a week, and a news agent may send in an order for 25 or 50 extra copies.

Of course in this as in any other matter it is a question of good faith. A leading newspaper has no interest in hiding its status or its number of subscribers, and the department must take their word. The weight is taken at intervals, and while, of course, the weight of the newspapers is not uniform from day to day, the Saturday issue being much heavier than the ordinary issues, very few errors are made in regard to the weight, by the postal officers. This business is followed very closely, and I can assure my hon. friend that no errors are made.
Is the Postmaster General quite certain that campaign literature, for instance, is not sent out in the bags furnished to the newspapers not prepaid?

These bags are examined at the office where they are sent, and we have an officer at the station where they are delivered to the postal clerk. As regards the adding of campaign literature, even the adding to a newspaper during a campaign, of special sheets printed say in
Toronto and sent to other papers is made the subject of a special charge for that weight. A member on this side of the House saw me in reference to that recently as a newspaper in his riding had been charged for campaign literature sent in this way, but the regulations of the department are such that such a charge could not be avoided.
The regulations are all right if the inspections are right.
The inspection is all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This resolution proposes to extend to a further amount the

aid which the government have been fox some years granting to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal. In former times the Harbour Commissioners issued their own debentures, but for some years now the government have been assisting the works of the Harbour Commissioners by lending them the government credit, thus enabling them to obtain the money at a much lower rate than they could raise it by the issue of their own debentures. The first loans were made bv the government at 3J per cent, and as the money market conditions improved the rate was reduced to 3 per cent. Now that money has become a little more expensive we are fixing the rate on the new loan at 3J per cent, the idea being that in each case the Harbour Commissioners shall be charged as nearly as may be what the money costs the government. The sums already authorized and loaned by the government being about exhausted, and there being still important work to be done, the commisssioners have applied for an extension of the amounts so to be loaned.
We are proposing by this resolution that further advances shall be made to them to the extent of $6,000,000. That will be distributed according to the plans of the commissioners, the time is not limited in the Bill, over a period of about three years. The purposes for which this loan is required are to extend the general system of harbour improvements, and terminal facilities, which is already at Montreal, and which, even in its present condition, has, I think, won in the highest degree the commendation of the people of Montreal, and of many others outside of Montreal, who are interested in the work to apply $100,000 to meet maturing debentures, which were issued years ago under the old system; and to extend the operations of the Harbour Commissioners, including wharf construction, deepening the harbour adjacent to the wharfs, lessening St. Mary's current by dredging, construction of sheds on wharfs, extension of the present harbour system of railway tracks, providing proper unloading facilities, and improved methods of handling cargoes. These in general terms indicate the nature of the works on which this money is to be expended. In every case, before expending the money the commissioners are obliged to submit their plans and specifications to the Governor in Council, and get their approval. The arrangement has worked very satisfactorily in the past. The present Harbour Commissioners are men who have met with the highest approval of the public interested in this great work, and I think the extension of this loan will meet with the favour of the House, and the country. I should add thaTThe interest on these loans has invariably been paid with promp-Mr. FIELDING.
titude. It is proposed, in accordance with the principle contained in the Railway Act, that during the period of construction, when no money can be earned, the interest on the sum advanced shall be deemed to be a part of the cost of construction. The interest on the sums which the government have advanced to the commissioners has been fully paid up to the 31st of December, last, so that the transaction as between the government, and the commissioners has been a very satisfactory one. The commissioners have had the aid of the government credit, the work has been well done, and I think the whole transaction is one that finds favour with parliament, and the country.
If I understand the hon. gentleman aright, he has not the plans of the proposed extension.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, not to cover fully the period of three years. The commissioners will only send us plans of the work from time to time. The plans for past works have been submitted before any money has been expended, and that will have to be done in the future; but no plans have yet been submitted under this Bill, though the general charter of the work proposed is understood.

I do not understand how they made an estimate of $6,000,000, unless they had plans. Information as t-o where this work is to be done, and how it is to be done fs very necessary. I was once on a committee appointed for the purpose of inquiring into the improvement of harbour facilities in the port of Montreal. A plan was then suggested for building new docks a little below St. Mary's current. The opinion I formed at the time was that all the money you may expend for docks, warehouses, and other facilities in Montreal, as at present proposed, will never accomplish anything, and that a big new plan ought to be adopted for building a large dock below the city, with warehouses alongside of it, and railway tracks on each side. I cannot of course speak of the present plans, as I know nothing about them; but I should judge from the remarks of the Finance Minister, that they are on the line of fixing up or tinkering with the works at present in Montreal. My opinion is, not that you should abandon these works, because they can be utilized, but that you should have a bigger scheme than you have at present. I would like to ask the minister what depth of water is to be provided for-35 feet or 30 feet?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The question of deepening the St. Lawrence channel is not in the hands of the commission. I think the Marine and Fisheries Department provides

thirty feet of water, though as to that I would not speak positively.

It is proposed to deepen Lake St. Peter to a depth of thirty-five feet, and you need at least the same depth in the harbour of Montreal. What I want to know is, are the commissioners providing a sufficient depth in the harbour to meet the new requirements of navigation on the St. Lawrence?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am quite sure they are; but when the Bill comes for a second reading, I shall be glad to give my hon. friend a more direct statement. I have no reason to complain of the operations of the Montreal Harbour Board on the ground that they are too small. They are quite comprehensive enough, considering the amount of money involved. The commissioners have outlined in a general way a scheme of harbour improvements which has been largely advertised in the public press. When I say that there are no plans, I mean that there are no plans that the government have approved of; but the commissioners have very large and generous views. They have plans which may not have attracted the notice of my hon. friend, and if it is desired that these plans should be brought here, I shall be glad .to have them brought. If we were called upon to approve of the whole scheme of the Montreal Harbour Board, it might call for a good deal more than $6,000,000; but the proposed works are entirely in line with a very comprehensive scheme which they have adopted after having made a very careful examination of harbour improvements and terminal facilities on the continent of Europe, in England and in America. So that I am sure that what they are doing is in accordance with a broad scheme, and is not a mere tinkering with the old conditions. But I shall be happy, when the Bill comes for a second reading, to bring all the information which my hon. friend desires.
Will the minister give us an idea of the amount of money already expended and the estimated expenditure after this whole scheme is completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The scheme, so far as the government is called upon to approve of it, contemplates this $6,000,000 extended over a period of three years. I do not say for a moment that that will be the end of it, because the business of Montreal, with the business of the whole Dominion, is developing rapidly, and I should not be surprised if at the end of three years there, should be a demand for a further sum; and I have no doubt that if the commissioners require it, and have paid interest in the meantime, parliament will be glad to provide it. But in providing for three years, I think we are looking as far forward as is
desirable at present. As to the amount of money already expended. The amount outstanding of debentures of the Montreal Harbour Commission i3 $13,142,000, of which debentures to the amount of $1,972,000 are held by the public; but the government loans, represented by debentures deposited by way of security, amount to $11,170,000, to which this $6,000,000 will now be added.
Do the proposed plans take into consideration the place below the rapids?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The limitations of the harbour have been enlarged. The scheme is in that respect a broad one, and some of the works are below St. Mary's current.
. Mr. SPROULE. If I understood the minister right, he said that we were not exactly loaning the money, but giving them the power to borrow on our credit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, we loan the money.
And we advance them the money?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
' A portion is to pay off the expiring debentures of the corporation at par value during 1910. To whom are -they payable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To the outside public, not to the government.
Then the Harbour Commissioners do issue debentures?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They did in former years, but they are not issuing any now, except for the purpose of depositing them with the government as security.
The interest payable on the debentures is receivable by the minister, and the commission pass their debentures over to the government in lieu of money?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In return for our advancing them the money they give us the debentures, which we hold as security.
There is nothing in the resolution to show the assent of His Excellency the Governor General?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is never found in the document itself. It is found in the intimation made to parliament when the resolution is moved, and that was made.

My hon. friend) said that of this $6,000,000, a portion is to be retained as before for the payment of interest during construction, and he intimated there were other portions in the same position. What is the amount which is retained by the government for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The sum so paid, iu the form of interest on construction, and therefore part of the capital, amounts to $355,000. As to what is to he paid after this, that will be a matter for the future.
What is liable to be paid at present on the sums borrowed before?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is nothing due. The matter has been adjusted to the 31st of December last. The total sum charged as interest during construction was $355,000. There is no interest account outstanding at present.
They borrowed a certain amount for construction before this $6,000,000 on similar terms. We have been paying ouTselves interest out of the amount we lent them. Has that total amount been paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, the matter was adjusted to the 31st of December last, and all interest properly chargeable in that way was charged up. The government received it by adjustment of the account, and the amount so charged, as distinct from the expenditure on the works themselves, was $355,000 There is no outstanding amount, no liability not dealt with in the way I-have described.
We have paid them out of the loan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. In the adjustment of the account they are entitled to charge up, as portion of the cost of thfe work, the interest on capital during construction just as would be done in case of a railway and for the same reason.
The work has been constructed and finished, and that ends it.

The hon. minister gave two sets of figures which represent thaij amount we have advanced up to the present to the commission, namely, $13,142,000 and $7,170,000. What is the explanation of the different figures?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The sum of $11,170,000 represents the amount which the government has lent to the Harbour Commission. The sum of $1,972,000 represents debentures held by the public and which were issued before the system was adopted of the government lending the money and the commission giving the government their debentures. As these $1,972,000 debentures fall due, the government will have to provide for them.
What interest do you receive on the $11,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On the first loan 3J per cpnt, on the others 3 per cent. The market Mr. J. G. HAGGART.
is, however, higher now and money costs us 3i per cent or a fraction more, so that we are charging 31 per cent on this loan.
Resolution reported, read the second time and agreed to.
Mr. FIELDING moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 191) to provide for further advances to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
Mr. FIELDING moved second reading.
I have no objection to the second reading, but before the third reading I would like to see the plan of the harbour, and what is proposed to. be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will see that whatever information is available of that kind will be on the table before the third reading.
When the late Mr. Tarte was Minister of Public Works, the government was represented on the commission and kept substantial control over the works. What control has the government now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At one time the Harbour Commissioners were rather numerous, representing various interests associated with the commerce of Montreal. Several years ago that system was changed, and the government appointed three commissioners who have the entire management. They are Major George Washington Stephens, Mr. C. C. Ballantyne and Mr. L. E. Geoffrion. They are appointed by the government, responsible to the government, and all plans and specifications and whatever they propose must be submitted to the Department of Marine and Fisheries before any work is done or money expended.
And assented to?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, it must receive the approval of the government before they can spend any of this money. I think this is as complete control as the government could have under a system of commission.
The government have no engineer in connection with this work? There is no revision except the nlans being submitted to the department to be examined here and approved?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The commission them-'selves have very capable and competent engineers to assist them. After their plans are completed and sent for approval they pass under the revision of engineers of the department, so I think the matter is 1 fairly guarded.
Who is the chief engineer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Cowie is the gentleman who has for many years been over this work, an engineer of high standing.
Are these commissioners paid by the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Out of harbour earnings. They are under control of the government and are paid out of harbour earnings.
Out of the appropriations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Out of earnings -charged to revenue.
Is this expenditure audited on behalf of the government? Is there control such, for instance, as examination by the Auditor General?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think not. We have followed, in that respect, the system which has been in existence for many vears. Perhaps there may be something to be said in favour of audit by the Auditor General. I have not had the matter brought to my attention before. It may be well worthy of consideration.

I should think it would be. It looks as if this were to be the government's property some day. Therefore, we shall not get the money back any more than if we had spent it directly on the work.
Mr.-FIELDING. I think there is something in that. Of course, the Harbour Commission have an efficient system of administration, and. no doubt, the matter is in good shape. There is a public report every year which is accessible. T will discuss with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who is the proper officer in charge, whether these accounts ought not to be submitted to the Auditor General.
How could you do that if the accounts are not paid out of consolidated revenue?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If we wish to do it, we could have the Auditor General given necessary power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
