House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Fisheries Act, chapter 45 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, by-
. (a) Defining the standard size of the barrel in which oysters are sold, bartered or trafficked in;
(b)	Prohibiting the taking, buying, selling, possessing or exporting of fish for the purpose of converting it into manure, guano, or fertilizer, or for its manufacture or conversion into oil or manure or other fertilizing product, without a permit from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries; and
(c)	Providing for the bringing into force, by proclamation, the regulations prepared by the International Fisheries Commission between Great Britain and the United States, now before the House, and to authorize the making of regulations to secure their enforcement, and fixing penalties for their violation. -Mr. Templeman.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Under the present Fishery Act, there is no provision as to the size of a barrel of oysters. Consequently, there is no assurance to the purchaser that in purchasing a barrel he will receive a certain quantity. One purpose of the Bill to be proposed will be to provide that a barrel of oysters shall be of equal dimensions with the barrel ordinarily used,for the sale of flour-seventeen inches diameter at the top or bottom, nineteen inches at the bulge and twenty-eight inches in height.
Another proposed amendment is to regulate the taking of fish to be used as a fertilizer. The present law provides that no one shall catch fish to be used for this purpose. That is too sweeping altogether, inasmuch as there are many fish that can well be used for fertilizing purposes. The proposition is to give the minister power to name fish that may be used) for manufacture into fertilizer.
It is proposed also, under the Bill to be submitted, to authorize by proclamation the regulations agreed upon under the International Fisheries Commission relating to the taking of fish in international waters.
What did the minister say with Tegard to the prohibition of the use of fish as fertilizer?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We propose to give the minister power to define the kind of fish that may be taken to be used for this manufacture. For instance, there are dogfish and other voracious fishes that are of no use for human food. The minister will have power to authorize the use of such fish for manufacture into fertilizer.
There nas been a discussion in the House two or three times
about dog-fish, and it was stated that they were being utilized for that purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: As a matter of fact the present Act is being violated every day, because they take dog-fish and utilize it as a fertilizer. I was asked the question if farmers might not use the surplus for manuring their lands, which I believe they are doing down in the maritime provinces. No doubt under the new provisions the minister will permit that to be done.

There are places in the maritime provinces where farmers are manuring the land with young shad and young salmon. They have weirs for catching fish, to which the farmer goes when the tide is out; he takes home for food what is large enough, and what is small he dumps into a cart and carries off to his farm for manure.

Dog-fish has been a great injury to the fishermen along the coast, both because it destroys the nets and destroys other fish, and it seems almost a hardship that a man must get permission from the minister before he is allowed to fake these fish and destroy them. The Act proposes to prohibit the tahing of dog-fish to be converted into oil or manure except on license by the government. I think that is not advisable. I think the destruction of dog-fish should be encouraged rather than discouraged. They make good oil and they make a good fertilizer. Along the shores of Northumberland Straits and in parts of the county I have the honour to represent, they catch these fish to a considerable extent and use them as a fertilizer. I am sure that if the minister were to take the views of the fishermen he would find that they are in favour of encouraging the destruction of this dog-fish as much as possible; and farmers would say that it is a hardship to them to have to get a permit to use dog-fish. I think it would be better to allow freedom in the destruction of these voracious fish that are of no use for food. There is another thing the Act should cover, and that is the wholesale destruction of useful fish by steam trawlers. They operate with large nets, and take great quantities of fish, of which they throw overboard those that are not useful for their purposes. A great waste is going on in that way. Fish that would be useful if allowed to escape are thus being destroyed, and the fisheries along our shores are being depleted by the use of these steam trawlers. Some provision should be made against the taking of these smaller fish, or if they are taken, they should be allowed to escape instead of being killed in nets and allowed to drift along the shore.

While this subject is being discussed I wish to draw the attention Mr. J. G. HAGGART.
of the minister to the taking of small and immature bar fish in the St. Lawrence. For years I have been drawing the attention of the department to this subject, and I have also had occasion to speak to Prof. Prince about the immense destruction of bar fish that is taking place. It is the finest fish we have in the St. Lawrence. They are caught by the thousand, but so small that the fishermen after catching them are ashamed to bring them on the market, and they sell them to pedlars who go about the country retailing them from house to house. They catch fish of from four to seven inches in length that are almost useless for food, nobody would dare to bring them on the market, because he would be laughed at; and so they are destroying that fish by the hundreds of thousands every year. It is really a pity, because it is one of the finest fish we have in the St. Lawrence, and attains a size of two or two and a half feet in length, and a weight of from six to nine pounds. Some stringent measures should be taken to prevent the fishermen selling this .fish to the pedlars for distribution. There should be a close inspection made, and nothing of that kind should be' allowed on the river. It is now allowed all the way down, the river on both shores for a distance of 60 or 75 miles. It is the finest fish we have in the St. Lawrence when allowed to mature, and I consider it a perfect scandal that they should be destroyed in this manner. The fish resemble the bass.

I wish to express the same view as my hon. friend from Anti-gonish (Mr. Chisholm). I think it will be a hardship to require the people who catch dog-fish along the coast first to get a permit from the authorities before they can use them for manure. I trust the minister will make an exception in the case of destruction of dog-fish and permit, not only the catching of them, but encourage it, because this fish is destroying the other fish that are of use. It is really one of the greatest scourges we have on the Atlantic coast. The dog-fish arrive in the summer time when the water gets warm; they come up from the south, they tear up tihe nets, they eat up the other fish that are in the nets, and practically the fishermen have to go out of business when the dog-fish arrive. The government has at present two or three places on the coast of the maritime provinces where these fish are purchased and turned into manure. This has been going on for a few years, and while it has lessened the quantity to some extent, still the Atlantic ocean is so large, and these fish are so numerous, that there will not be any material lessening of them by means of these establishments. A

great number of them, however, are being caught and turned to some useful purpose. It is also not an uncommon thing for fish to decay before they are taken out of the water. Occasionally a fisherman's net sinks, and when he is able to find it, with a quantity of fish in it, they are of no use except for manure. The difficulty of going for a permit in isolated cases of this kind would be great, and I trust that in the regulations which may be made the minister will keep that in mind. The idea of the minister is a good one. He wishes to preserve the fisheries, and of course we all agree in that object. But I trust the regulations will permit exceptions to be made in the case of destructive fish, and also in eases where it would be to the advantage of everybody that these fish that are not fit for food may be used as manure. I also agree with my hon. friend from Antigonish in what *he says of steam trawlers. The steam trawlers operating on the banks are chiefly owned outside of Canada; they are increasing in number. A few years ago they were almost unknown on our coast, although there are many of them in in use in Britain and in the North Sea. But they are coming across the Atlantic now to operate on the banks of Newfoundland, and along the coast of Nova Scotia. They are very destructive engines. They catch not only the mature fish that are fit for food, but they also catch the small ones. The trawler is a steamboat that drags a large net along the bottom of the sea, with a wide mouth, and it takes in everything, both small and large. The small ones are crushed to pieces at the end of the net, and I suppose twenty-five per cent of the fish caught in these trawlers are of no use whatever for food, because they are too small and immature. I think you will find, on investigation, that they have destroyed the fisheries to a large extent in the North sea, and it would be a good thing if we could keep .them away from the Atlantic coast altogether. It would require, of course, international arrangements to do that. I have no doubt that the government of the United States would be quite willing to enter into arrangements by which these trawlers would be prohibited on the banks and along the coast of eastern Canada. I have drawn the matter to the attention of the minister on several occasions. As the hon. member for Antigonish has mentioned it, I merely wish to say that I am in full accord with him, and I would like to see something done in that connection.

Why is it necessary that there should be a permit issued by the government to enable persons to catch
these deleterious fish, that are such an injury to other fish, and sell them for manure?

I quite agree with my hon. friend that there should be no permit necessary in the case of fish that are not fit for food and are better destroyed. Of course, it is different in the case of mackerel, herring, codfish or any of the food fishes. If these food fishes are caught and used as fertilizer it should be stopped, but 1 trust that the minister will not ask for any permit for catching and destroying fish that are better destroyed,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The proposed regulations prepared by the commission were brought down in the shape of a return, and have been printed and circulated.
What was it that the minister referred to in answering my hon. friend from Selkirk? He spoke of fishery regulations.
Those were in reference to Manitoba.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Those were local
regulations in reference to Lake Winnipeg, while these have reference to international fisheries in boundary waters. These are the regulations framed by Professor Prince and Mr. Jordan, the two commissioners.
Have these international regulations been brought down to the House?	'

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Yes, they were
brought down in the shape of a return, and they have been printed. The treaty undex which these regulations have been framed provides that they shall be brought into force by joint proclamation of the two governments at a date to be fixed in the future. I assume that they will be brought into force in time for the fishing operations of this year, but this resolution provides that the Fishery Act may be amended in such a way as to empower the government to proclaim these fishery regulations. It has been deemed advisable by the Justice De-

partment that the power of proclaiming these regulations as law should be in the Act. I may say, in regard to what my hon. friends from Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm) and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) have said in connection with the catching of these voracious fish, that it is thought necessary to have some amendment to the present law. The present law reads that ' No one shall catch fish for the purpose of using it as manure '; consequently, every person who takes dog-fish and converts it into fertilizer is violating the Act as it stands. Our desire is to amqnd that clause and give the minister power to define what fish or marine animals may be used as fertilizer. If it is done by means of permit, there will be no difficulty in granting permits to any persons who want them. It is merely to define what fish and marine animals may be used for this purpose. I know that at the present moment on the Pacific ocean there is a company aiming at the capturing of sea-lion, hair-seal and dog-fish for the purpose of converting them into fertilizer. There is no question that a permit should be given to any person who will capture and^ convert them into fertilizer.
I am advised with regard to trawlers, that as soon as a trawler was brought to this coast from Europe-I believe there is only one on the Atlantic coast at the present time-an order in council was passed prohibiting the operation of that trawler within the three-mile limit and within bays. I -would assume that outside of the three-mile limit, this government has no control, and it would be a matter of international regulation. At all events, within the three-mile limit the use of trawlers, which my hon. friends say is very destructive to fish, has been prohibited.

It is quite true that an order in council has been passed prohibiting the operation of these trawlers within the three mile limit. It is also true that as far as the Canadian parliament is concerned it has not jurisdiction beyond the three mile limit. That is a matter of international regulation. But, I submit that the time has come when the department or the government might seriously consider the making of some international arrangement whereby the operation of these trawlers could be prevented or controlled. It is a fact that along the shores of Nova Scotia the fishermen have to set their trawls outside the three mile limit; they have to go five or six miles out. I know that along the shores of Antigonish county when the steam trawler ' Wren,' was operating last year, and the year before the fishermen had to take up their gear because they were afraid it would be destroyed by the steam trawler. The regulation which has been passed, and which exhausts the jurisdiction of the govem-Mr. TEMPLEMAN.
rnent in the matter does not to any substantial extent protect our fishermen along the shores. Those engaged in the cod fishery practically had to give up business last year, and the year before. Their gear was threatened with destruction by this trawler. The trawler, while manoeuvring during its operations, will destroy the nets of the fishermen without those in control of it being conscious of the fact, and I would urge upon the acting minister, as I have urged upon the minister, that the matter be taken up as soon as possible, and some regulations brought about to prevent the operation of the trawler within ten miles, or, at all events, within six miles of the coast. The order in council prohibits fishing within the bays, and harbours of Canada, but what is the meaning of bays and harbours? The Americans have put a certain construction on it. They claim it means three miles from the shore, following the sinuosities of the coast. The Canadians have always contended that the three mile limit means three miles outside of the land measuring from headland to headland. If the Canadian interpretation were followed it would not make so bad a situation for our fishermen, but as it is, the practice being to follow the sinuosities of the shore in determining the extra territorial limit our fishermen are subjected to great annoyance and injury by these trawlers. I would request that an endeavour should be made to prevent this. This government it is contended could control its own sub-jetcs, and make it illegal for any Canadians to engage in this kind of fishing which is very destructive. But if such an attempt were made the same thing would happen here as happened in the old country. The moment Canadians were forbidden to fish in trawlers, they would fly some other flag, possibly the French flag. A number of French trawlers are fishing on the banks outside the three mile limit, and the department could not stultify itself by prohibiting Canadians from what other French and other fishermen do. A regulation of that kind was passed in Scotland some time ago, and the instant it was done Scotch and English trawlers registered in a Norwegian port flew the Norwegian flag, and then they could fish outside the three mile limit of Scotland with impunity. The only way to relieve the situation, and save the fishermen is to have some international regulation made prohibiting the operation of trawlers at least within six miles or ten miles of our coast.

My reading of the regulations would be that a time is already fixed in 3ome instances for the coming into force of the regulations. In my section the fishermen are relying on the wording of

the regulations as given out by Dr. Starr Jordan and Professor Prince, and are governing themselves accordingly. For example with reference to the size of a mesh for taking small fish in Lake Ontario we are told:
No gill net or other movable net of less than four and three-fourths inches mesh, extension measure, as actually used in fishing, shall be drawn, set, placed, or maintained for whitefish or lake trout in these treaty waters.
No gill net or other movable net of less than three and one-eighth inches mesh, extension measure, as actually used in fishing, shall be drawn, set, placed or maintained in Lake Erie-
And this is the part to which I more particularly refer:
*-or of less than two and one-half inches mesh in Lake Huron, Lake Superior, and Lake Ontario, for fish other than whitefish or lake trout.
The above restrictions shall take effect on and after January 1, 1911.
The fishermen in my section quite under' stand that whatever may be done by the government in the way of a proclamation these regulations shall not be brought into force, at least those in regard to the size of the net, until January 1, 1911. I understand that the minister proposes to authorize under an Act of parliament a proclamation declaring when these regulations shall come into force. It is important that these regulations shall not be brought into force at once. The fishermen have large quantities of nets on hand, and if they are compelled to use a mesh even one-eighth of an inch larger than what they are using now, it would be a serious matter for them, as they would have to throw away their nets and purchase new ones. I hope the minister will not bring the regulations into force at an earlier date than January 1, 1911; I would rather impress on him the necessity for extending the time for bringing these regulations into force for another year. The nets the fishermen now have will last ror two years from the first of January last, and it would be only fair to the fishermen to allow them to use their present nets until they are worn out, especially a3 the difference in size is so very slight,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The authority that is taken under the resolution is to empower the Governor General by proclamation to bring into force the international regulations prepared by the International Fisheries Commission appointed under the treaty signed at Washington, April 11, 1908, between Great Britain and the United States concerning the fisheries in waters contiguous to Canada and the United States. With regard to the date on which these regulations shall be brought into force, if I remember rightly, under the treaty both governments have to proclaim them as taking effect on a certain date. We
might, with the concurrence of the United States government, fix the first of January 1911 as that date. It is quite true, as my hon. friend says, that the first of January, 1911, is mentioned in one of the regulations as the date on which it shall take effect, which is rather peculiar, in view of the fact that the regulations might not be proclaimed until after that date. However, I think it is the desire of both the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and of the United States government that these regulations should be proclaimed so as to have effect during the fishing Season of 1911. It is not deemed possible to have the regulations effective before that date, and therefore it is not at all probable that they will be proclaimed as taking effect before that.

What time of the year would the hon. minister consider to be the fishing season? The class of fishing to which I refer is carried on all the year round, except perhaps during the warmer weather in summer. Some of the regulations may be brought into force sooner than others; but there would be nothing lost to the department by extending the time even for another year in the case of the regulation to which I refer, as there is only 4 of an inch difference in the size of the nets. I hope that the minister, in preparing any legislation in regard to this matter, will deal as leniently with the fishermen as he possibly can.

When the minister said that there was only one trawler operating on our coast, I presume he meant one Canadian trawler. There has been a large increase in this method of fishing in the last few years. In 1907, according to statistics which I have, there were seven French trawlers which came across the Atlantic and operated on the banks of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland; in 1908 there were fourteen ; and last year there were about thirty. They have been a great annoyance to the regular fishermen on the coast, both Canadian and American, and I am informed that there are no other trawlers at all operating on the Atlantic coast. These trawlers are nearly all owned in France, and they are invading our waters. These banks on the coast of Nova Scotia are the breeding ground of the codfish and -the haddock, which are the most valuable fish we have; and if they continue to operate there, I have no doubt that these valuable fisheries will be destroyed. Therefore,^ I wish i to impress upon the acting Minister of Marine and Fisheries and on the Prime Minister the importance of dealing with this question if there is any possibility of obtaining international arrangements by which these trawlers will be prohibited from operating on the banks. A few years ago arrangements were made

by which the seal fisheries of the Pacific coast were protected by international law, and I consider that the protection of the breeding grounds of the codfish and the haddock on the Atlantic coast is of equal importance. I have the best reason for believing that the government of the United States would join with the government of Canada in anything that- could be done to prohibit that mode of fishing. The banks on which these fish are found are not very large or numerous. They are confined to a few hundred miles, and there is a large fleet of Canadian and American vessels engaged on these banks. The fishermen's method of fishing is to put their gear into the water, leave it for a time, and then take it up. In the meantime, these trawlers come along and destroy it, so that when the fishermen take un their gear, they find only a few remnants left, and often their whole outfit is swept away. I trust that the matter will be dealt with seriously, and that if possible international arrangements will be made to control or prohibit parties engaged in this destructive method of fishing.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The question which my hon. friend has raised is a very large one, of an international character, and we cannot at the moment make any declaration. If we are going to have regulations dealing with trawl fishing, there is no doubt that it will be necessary for the United States, Great Britain, France and all other countries engaged in that industry to participate. I do not know whether in the past any negotiations have taken place looking for the regulation of trawl fishing. I am aware that trawlers are coming to both the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts. We have power to regulate them only within the three-mile limit, and that has been done on foot-n coasts. I will direct the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to the observations of my hon. friend in 'Hansard', and will impress upon him the importance of giving full consideration to this question.

I wish to ask the minister if the regulations set out in this return have been adopted by the American government without any change beyond what is shown here. I understand that some objection was taken to them and that efforts were made to have some changes made in them.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The regulations have not been adopted by either government and will not be adopted until they are proclaimed concurrently bv both governments. The regulations as printed were agreed to by the two commissioners, and it simply remains for the sanction of both governments to make them law. That, I understand, is the present position Mr. SINCLAIR
Has there been any change made by Professor Prince, and the representative of the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No.
The regulations stand just as they are?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I understand so.
Has the American government made representations1 asking for changes?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Not to the knowledge of the department.
Is it the intention of the department to stand by these regulations or does it intend permitting changes to be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The intention is to proclaim these regulations just as soon as the United States government do. We must act concurrently. The regulations become the law of both countries on the same day, but I think the treaty provides [DOT] that changes may be made from year to year on the unanimous decision of the commissioners.

This return shows what regulations are agreed upon between the two commissioners, but I understand that representations have been made to Washington by some parties interested in the United States to have changes made, and Professor Prince has been in Washington again. I would like to know, because some of my constituents are interested, whether it is the intention of the government to permit any changes?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am informed that the department has no knowledge of any proposal to make any change, and does not know that the American fishing interests are asking foT any. I would assume that, as the regulations have been agreed to, no changes will be made, but I think the treaty itself provides for the making of changes from year to year on the unanimous consent of the commission.

The United States government virtually say in the treaty that they are going to secure the assent of the various states interested to a proclamation carrying into effect these international regulations. The minister is no doubt aware that, so far as the great lakes are concerned, any property rights in the fisheries belong to the states, and are held by the states, and that the various states have different regulations. For instance the regulations of New York state, on Lake Ontario, and those on Lakes Erie and Huron, are different. It was suggested, at the time the treaty was made, that it would be advisable to have the control, and the regu-

lation, and the governing power vested in the federal government. I have followed this question, and I cannot see that the American government has secured the consent of the state governments to permit the federal government to deal with the fisheries on the Great Lakes at all; and until such time as the federal government of the United States has secured that consent,
I do not see how it can have any status at all in the matter. Why then should we make any regulations with them at all of an international character? We have taken power to make international regulations. It seems to me we are travelling a little far in agreeing with the United States to do certain things, when the Americans can back out of their agreement by saying that the state rights interfere, but will insist all the same on our sticking to our bargain. Another point is that the Americans have not taken any steps towards a close season.
I do not see that any attempt is made under these regulations to have a close season at all. To my mind it is absolutely necessary for the protection of our fisheries that there should be a close season. In looking over the regulations, I find that the American position is that assumed by them all the way through. Is it the intention of our government to go into a deal of this kind with the federal government of the United States without that government having the authority from the various states to carry out its bargain?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: My understanding of the question of jurisdiction in the United States is that while the various states have control over the fisheries within those states, when the United States government make a treaty with a foreign country, that treaty supersedes state rights. I believe that such is the opinion of the Washington government.
What authority has the hon. minister for that statement? The entirely opposite view was taken with reference to the Sault Ste. Marie Falls.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I understand that is the view of the Justice Department at Washington.
Where do you find it?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is catechising me on a legal point. But it is not at all likely that the United States government would have entered into, this agreement unless the federal authorities thought they could enforce the regulations they were preparing.

Has the minister read the correspondence brought down last session on the matter? The correspondence shows that the federal government 'hopes'
to secure the co-operation of the state governments.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am stating the international aspect of the question, _ as I understand it. Whether I got that impression from the public press or from some return or document, I am not sure.
It is just an inspiration.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Why would the federal government at Washington appoint a commissioner, and enter into a compact with Canada to do certain things, if they did not believe they had the power to enforce their regulations?

The documents show that they say they 'hope' to be able to get the various state interests to consent. If the various states consent to allow the federal government to deal with the matter, then the federal government may act to some purpose, but they have not done so.

My hon. friend is not a little mistaken in the view he takes. The states of the union are not in the position of riparian owners in the case of water rights. They are in exactly the same position as the northwestern provinces in this confederation. The federal government is the owner of all riparian rights, not only in the lands but in the water.
What is the hon. member's authority for that?

The constitution of the United States, and the fact that the states of the union are not owners of the land as are the old provinces of Canada. I think my hon. friend will not pretend to dispute that.
The hon. member (Mr. Conmee) cannot quote a single case in United States jurisprudence to bear out his statement.
I can put the matter the other way-the hon. member (Mr. J. A. Currie) cannot find any evidence to the contrary.

I will give an instance. At Sault Ste. Marie, the state of . Michigan had granted water rights to a certain portion of St. Mary's falls to a private individual. These power rights became vested in a company or syndicate. When the Waterways Commisison endeavoured to treat with the St. MaTy's falls, a protest was entered, the matter was fought out and the decision of the court was that the riparian rights belong to the state, and not to the federal authority.

The hon. member is entirely mistaken; the facts of the case are

not as he has stated. What happened on the American side is pretty much what happened on the Ontario side. The province of Ontario gave a charter for the development of power on the Canadian side. The state of Michigan did the same. To give that development on both sides, the company* got United States federal authority. The action of the courts to which my hon. friend refers upheld, not the authority of the state, but, the authority of the private owner. But the state itself was not the riparian owner. The American courts have held that the riparian owner, if a private party or company who have purchased from the state-that is, from the federal government-has an interest in the riparian rights which has to be satisfied. That case is not fought out yet, but I think it is conceded that the riparian owner, whether individual or company, must be compensated for his rights.
From whom did the owner get his title?
From the federal government of the United States?
No, from the state of Michigan.
He got legislation from Michigan
He got his title there.

How could he get the title from Michigan to develop a power, when the state of Michigan did not own the land? All the land is sold through the medium of the United States. The state of Minnesota, except with regard to land that has been given to it for school and other purposes, does not own the soil of the state. And the state of Michigan is in the same position.

I am sorry for the hon. member (Mr. Conmee), for he is very much astray. The case he cites shows only that he has not the faintest, hazy idea of the situation. The fact is that the state of Michigan gave that power to a private individual and granted the land under the river in fee. The case has been fought out, and it has been decided that if the federal government takes over a water right, it must compensate that owner. As to what the hon. member said about a state of the union not owning the land, there is no state in the union that will submit to have its ownership of its own soil challenged.

The hon. member (Mr. J. A, Currie) is entirely ignorant of the history of the United States. 1 do not say that what I have been contending in this matter applies to such states as the state of New York. But, as to the state of Michigan, the state of Minnesota and
others, they are in exactly the same position as our own northwestern provinces- they do not own the land at all.
Who owns the water-powers of New York on the St. Lawrence- the state authority or the federal?
I will not speak as to the state of New York, for it was a Crown colony before it became a state.
It has been decided that the power rests and is vested in the state of New York.

My hon. friend (Mr. J. Haggart) has heard information read in this House which ought to give him light on that subject. The state of New York has no nower over and cannot give control of the St. Lawrence river. It has no legislative jurisdiction over it. It gave a waterpower to the very company over whose Bill we sat up all night recently, but before the right was complete, it had to be ratified at Washington.

But surely the hon. member knows the distinction. The federal authority has rights of legislation in regard to navigation, and, so far as state rights interfere with that of the federal authority, they are set aside. But all the profits that come from the users of water-powers on the St. Lawrence in the United States belong to the state adjoining.

No, that has been fought out in the United States very fully. The most important case arose on the Michigan side of the river at Detroit, over a question of building docks. It was held that the riparian owner had certain rights which must be satisfied before even the government of the United States could place a dock there. Now, that is not quite the case on our side. In this country the Crown can assume control of that very well.
How could a private individual get his right-from the federal authority?
I assume so.

The hon. member is drifting to his water-powers again. I don't like to get into these water-power deals. Let us keep to the point. What authority in the United States is it that issues the fishing licenses on the Great Lakes?

My hon. friend (Mr. J. A. Currie) has water on the brain to-day.
I am not responsible for what the various states may have done. The provinces in this Dominion have issued fishing regulations, and the province of Ontario collects

a license fee for fishing. The states of the union do the same.
I might suggest that as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) is now in his place, he might be allowed to assume his role.
The hon. member (Mr. J. Haggart) wants a higher authority than myself? I am quite willing.

The question simply is whether the states consent to give the whole jurisdiction to the federal authority. That is a simple question, and I am sure the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) will recognize not only how simple it is, but how pertinent to the subject under discussion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The question the hon. member has put is a fair one. I believe that, at the present time, the accepted doctrine in the United States is that the treaty-making power is the paramount authority and supervenes the rights of the states. I do not agree in everything that has been said by the hon. member for Simcoe with regard to the rights of the states and the rights of the federal government. But in this matter I think it is now accepted that the treaty power of the United States is the supreme authority and supersedes the rights of the states.

No doubt that is the authority under which the arrangements were made. The federal power of making a treaty supersedes state rights, and the federal government contend that they have the power to enter into negotiations of this kind although the property may belong to the state.
Resolution reported, read the second time and agreed to.
Mr. TEMPLEMAN moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 192) to amend the Fisheries Act.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Mr. OLIVER, in moving the second reading of Bill (No. 125) to amend the Land Titles Act. said: The registration of titles in unorganized territory is provided for by this government. In what is now called the Northwest Territories, that is to say, the country lying north of the three prairie provinces, provision is made in the Land Titles Act for registration within that territory. There has been very little granting or transfer of titles in that territory up to the present time, but a condition has arisen where the actual title has been earned, and it is desirable that the title 188
should be granted. No provision has yet been made for the registration of title within those territories, and no such provision is possible without an amendment of the Act. The conditions are such, there being so very few titles to register, that it is not thought advisable to establish a registry office within that territory at the present time, and we ask for an amendment to the Act to allow the titles in the Northwest Territories to be registered at Ottawa. It is simply a temporary provision, until progress requires the establishment of an office actually within the territory.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, considered in committee, reported, read the third time and passed.

Mr. OLIVER moved the second reading of Bill (No. 141) to amend the Indian Act. He said: This Bill contains three clauses, the provisions of each of which are entirely distinct. The first clause provides for the better protection of Indian lands. It is, of course, an understood principle, that the Indians have the sole right of occupation of their reserves. But in the opinion of the Justice Department, the procedure whereby that exclusive right of occuoancy is to be exercised-the procedure by which it may be enforced, is not altogether efficient, and it is on the advice of that department that I am asking for this amendment. The second section relates to contracts made by the Indians which would obligate their band or communal funds. While it has always been an understood principle of the Indian Act that band funds or Indian property, that is, tribal property, cannot be obligated by any agreement entered into by the Indians except with the approval of the government-although that has been the understanding, there seems to have arisen some question about it, and it is thought desirable to remove that question by he provision of section 2.
Has this an ex post facto effect?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, it would not have any ex post facto effect.
It might have.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It was not intended to have. Section 3 is intended to put beyond' question the absolute right of the Indian to the money that he is entitled to receive' from the government; that is to say, to de-' clare that it is. not subject to attachment by legal process.

I do not yet seem to be very clear with regard to the first clause.



It applies where there is a dispute between an individual, a corporation or other parties and the Indians as to the ownership of land?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
That has to be decided by the Exchequer Court?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
What court has jurisdiction at the present moment?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That seems to have been the difficulty. While the law declares the position, the procedure is not defined. This is designed to provide the procedure.
Is this clause intended to apply to the difficulty which at present exists with reference to the Oka Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

It would apply to it. The jurisdiction seems to be exercised by the local courts in Quebec as to the ownership of that particular property. Now the jurisdiction is removed from the local to the Exchequer Court. It may be the better plan, but we want to know the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly. It has not any reference to the Oka case. In that case the question before the courts is: Is that an Indian reserve? One step in the procedure has been taken, and as the House knows, we have made arrangements to carry the case to the Privy Council. This legislation is not dealing with that case at all.

It would be very reasonable to suppose that this legislation does apply. It says:
If the possession of any lands reserved or claimed to be reserved by the Indians is withheld, or if any such lands are adversely occupied or claimed by any person.
The question is to be determined by the Exchequer Court. This statute, I would take it, would apply to all such cases in future. These cases have been pending in other courts for some time.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would think that if the Oka case had not been in the courts then possibly this would apply, but, of course, the Oka case having been entered in the court and being under judicial investigation-
The last dispute with the Indians is not in the court at all; it only occurred a month or two ago.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is a stated case before the courts for the purpose of settling, the question as to whether this is an In-1 dian reserve or not. I would take it for granted that so long as that case is under consideration and until it has reached, its Mr. J. G. HAGGART.
conclusion it would not be proper that this legislation should intervene. But it will be clear that if there is a necessity for such legislation, and in our estimation there is a necessity for it, we cannot very well postpone it, because there happens to be a case in the court which might be affected by it. If there is any danger of a clash I would much rather have the exception declared in the Bill, but my understanding is that it is not necessary.
The Minister of Justice is right at the minister's hand, and this seems to be of sufficient importance to get the advice of the Justice Department on it.

I would like to ask the minister to leave this Bill over and not put it through to-night, as there are some members of the House who are not present, and who would like to be present, when the Bill is passed,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: On the point raised, my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) understands that the rule is that cases under procedure are not affected by a law made after the proceedings were instituted. That is his view, and I think it is certainly fair and no doubt is good law.

Ex post facto legislation would be interpreted in the strictest sense in favour of the contention that the legislation should not apply. The point is this:	Disputes have arisen between the
Indians and parties there with reference to the cutting of wood. The question as to the right of cutting wood, or of the ownership of the property, has not yet gone to the courts, and it would, under this legislation, have to come to the Exchequer Court. I think that all cases in dispute as to ownership with respect to Indian lands must be decided1 by this court.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the intention.

I notice that section 2 declares that:
No contract or agreement binding or purporting to bind, or in any way dealing with the moneys or securities referred to in this section .... shall be valid or of any force or effect, unless and until it has been approved in writing by the superintendent general.
That would cover the annuities paid to Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Consequently they cannot barter off their rights without getting the consent of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the purpose we have in view.
I thought that was the law now?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Everybody supposed that was the law, but apparently there has been some mistake on the subject, and we want to make it the law unquestionably. It is not introducing a new principle; it is merely affirming a well recognized and accepted principle.
Has this an ex post facto effect?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

This would not cover applications of money made in an unjustifiable manner with the partial consent of the department of roads, or repairs, or anything of that kind without the full legal consent of the Indians to it? It does not cover the past; it is intended for the future.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would think that it could not legally cover the past, and certainly in administration I would say that it should not and that it is only in the future that it should have effect.
Is this law intended to apply to Indian lands in the older provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes

I do not quite appreciate why the right of trying a question between an Indian and an ordinary man in Nova Scotia should be removed from the Supreme Court. Does this take away the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to try a dispute with reference to land or trespass which might be a very slight matter? I believe that questions of that kind should be tried in the Supreme Court of the province without going to the Exchequer Court which with U3 is regarded as a very clumsy remedy. We do not have the Exchequer Court in the province more than once in two years, and to secure a remedy from it is considered rather difficult. It is true we do not often have suits with Indians, but we would like to have the right to settle them when they do arise in the same manner as ordinary suits. As to whether the law is retroactive or not I quite agree that it is not retroactive unless it is specifically made so, but it is a different proposition when you come to deal with jurisdiction. With regard to rights it would not be retroactive, but on the question of jurisdiction of the courts it would be retroactive.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,
This preserves all the old procedure and remedies, and at the same time enacts this new remedy?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I take it that this would allow an action for trespass or a minor action to be taken before the local courts, but a more important case would come before the Exchequer Court.

The intention of the section should be more clearly stated.
On section 2,
This certainly is ex post facto. It must certainly apply to some agreements made in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If my hon. friend thinks that is so, and it can be guarded against by words added, I would be quite willing to guard against it.

While the minister is amending the Indian Act, has he considered the advisability of amending section 89 of the Act? That section provides for the control of money arising from the sale of an Indian reserve, and provides in effect that not more than fifty per cent of these proceeds can be given to the Indians. It seems to me that there might be cases in which it would be advantageous for the government to have a discretion as to giving a larger proportion to the Indians directly, instead of funding it for their benefit. For instance the question of the Song-hees reserve in Victoria is a burning one and great difficulty has been found in making a settlement with the Indians to get them off the reserve. As a matter of fact, although there have been many efforts there has been no result. It has been my opinion that one of the sticking points is that the Indians cannot see where they are going to get a sufficient inducement in cash at the present time. If one of the contentions put forward by these Indians for their desire to remain on that land is correct it seems to me there is no reason why they should not get a larger proportion, if not the whole of the purchase money directly. They contend that a number of their young men and women are working in factories and other places in the town, and it is a convenient place for them to live, and they do not want to be disturbed. If they are sufficiently enlightened to work in the factories they are able to take care of their funds. If the section were amended by striking out the words * not exceeding fifty per cent ' and leaving it discretionary with the Governor in Council to deal with the funds either by funding them, or handing them over to the Indians, it might be a step towards a settlement of that very vexed question.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It would be contrary to the established policy of the government of Canada in dealing with Indians to treat

Indians generally in that way. It is generally considered that there should be a permanence of revenue from any property which the Indians have, and the Act as it stands, allowing 50 per cent to be paid directly, is a big step in advance of the Act as it formerly was, and I doubt if it would be acceptable generally to allow a larger proportion to be paid. I quite appreciate the very difficult character of the conditions which my hon. friend has in mind. I would very much rather provide for that particular case, which is very exceptional, by a special Act, than to amend the general Act to meet a special case.

If one could have a positive assurance that a special Act would be brought down to deal with that case, there would possibly be no necessity for making this amendment. But I have no doubt that is not the only case. I know that there is a case within the limits of the city of Vancouver, and the people there are very anxious to get rid of that reserve. Not very long ago the Minister of the Interior made an effort to settle with
the Indians in regard to this particular reserve. He was prepared to>
offer them a certain sum in cash, amounting to $2,000 per family for 40 families. The Indians were asking for more, but the minister said, I cannot go any further, because I can only give you 50 per cent of the value of the reserve. That being the case, if such an amendment as that proposed were made, it would materially assist the settlement of that question.
Progress reported.

What business will be taken up on the first day after the vacation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will continue on the Bills which have been discussed today, and which we have not been able to put through-the minor Bills. Almost anything except the Naval Bill will be taken up on the opening day.
